extracted.intended_audience: academic advertising researchers and industry advertising/media practitioners (advertising managers, media planners)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for designing, validating, and using academic research on advertising (laboratory and field) to inform media planning, segmentation, and message strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for combined communications factors and interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The communications process can be understood only if one takes into account the combined effects of the source, channels, message, and audience factors; as well as the possible interactions among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying repetition or other message effects, researchers should not treat number of exposures in isolation but include other factors (buyer segments, product types, brands, ad formats or illustrations, colors, schedules, appeals, competitive activities, and media mixes) that make up the whole communications situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate laboratory techniques against field experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The results in the laboratory would be useful, however, only if they were transferable to an actual situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare multiple laboratory studies with large field experiments — the report cites eight separate studies compared with a large field experiment, which indicated the laboratory technique produced results comparable to the field; only validated lab techniques should be used to predict campaign effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor media scheduling to campaign goals and response type
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals of an advertising campaign should constitute criteria for media scheduling decisions; since the effectiveness of different schedules depends upon the type of desired advertising response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition-response curves differ by response measured (attention, learning, attitude, behavior); schedules must account for possible S-shaped curves, thresholds, and wearout (including curves that turn down due to boredom or irritation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure multiple types of advertising response
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific types of responses that were investigated were attention, learning, attitude, behavioral intention, and overt behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate measures for each response: attention (physiological equipment), learning (recognition and recall tests), attitude (attitude scales), overt behavior (simulated buying situations). Match measures to campaign objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge segmentation criteria by practical usefulness for media/message selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposed basis for identifying or segmenting a market must be judged in terms of its usefulness in media and message selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Can individuals in the defined market be reached efficiently by specific media? Do the criteria provide a basis for selecting appeals or designing persuasive messages? If not, the segmentation basis may be of limited practical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider life-style variables as a meaningful segmentation basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Life-style variables (activities, interests, opinions, values, goals, situational forces) can describe an individual's 'life style' and be meaningful bases for classifying consumers into market segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life-style groups may differ in information sources used, degree of deliberation, family participation, and perceived risk; these differences inform promotion mix and media choices. The Syracuse study found significant, actionable differences between urban and rural purchasers of a new durable good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test general communications models before applying to advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many research findings in the general communications literature deal with types of communication other than advertising, an advertiser who applies such research must assume that the results can be generalized to an advertising context—but this assumption may not be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to test transferability; do not uncritically apply general communication models to advertising because advertising may possess unique properties that change how content is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental designs that vary message form with identical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Present subjects with messages in the form of ads, news stories, memos, and letters; messages of identical content are presented in different forms to measure the influence of form on perception of message content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control content while varying form; include test items (e.g., 'accurate' vs 'inaccurate' statements, logical derivations vs unrelated statements) to detect differences in acceptance or inference attributable to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for advertising-specific interpretive biases (tolerance for favorable but illogical inferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals tend to accept logically invalid statements to a greater extent when message content is presented in the form of an advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should note that people may infer advertiser intent and accept favorable but logically unsupported statements; this 'tolerance' affects how advertising is perceived and must be considered when interpreting experimental and survey results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research should span diverse situational variables when studying repetition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Study repetition effects across different buyer segments, product types, brands, ad formats or illustrations, colors, schedules, appeals, competitive activities, and media mixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because repetition effects interact with many situational factors, experimental programs should be designed broadly enough to capture these interactions rather than relying on narrow, single-condition studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate grant program success by scholarly output and capacity building
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant program produced doctoral dissertations, numerous journal articles and working papers; graduate students benefited and pursued research and teaching careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider quality of research output (papers, presentations), student training outcomes, and whether grants attracted additional academic support (seed money) when assessing the value of research funding programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge practical limitations to applying research in business settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied research information is seldom neutral; timeliness, decision-process structure, and reward systems in firms can impede the usefulness and adoption of research findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research with awareness of business constraints: deliver actionable results on useful timelines, consider how findings will be used within organizational decision processes, and address incentives that might discourage adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link integrated (racially inclusive) advertising research to segment-level sales outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners had not investigated reactions of black consumers to advertising depicting both black and Caucasian models; nor had they tried to relate such integrated advertising to overall sales or sales within racial segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying integrated advertising, measure consumer reactions by racial segment and attempt to relate inclusive creative to sales or segment-specific performance rather than relying on social-rationale explanations alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray minority groups authentically to improve ad effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mexican-American respondents indicated that inclusion was favorable, especially when Mexican-Americans were portrayed as purposeful and hard-working in everyday life situations; avoidance of racial caricatures and stereotypes was stressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages that depict minority groups in dignified, realistic roles; avoid caricature and stereotype to increase perceived effectiveness among the target community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience economic optimism when designing prejudice-reduction advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who were more optimistic about the future were more favorably inclined toward advertising designed to reduce prejudice than were the more pessimistic respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns aiming to reduce racial prejudice (e.g., 'brotherhood' advertising) may be most effective among audiences with favorable economic expectations; audience segmentation by economic outlook can inform message targeting.
